Equiloc Quad 2Tri 120

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: two equal-sided triangles are built on a four-sided shape, and their two top tips land on one point on the blue line.
How to play: Drag S around the circle, or C and D along the sloping lines. You can also focus a point and use the arrow keys; tick the boxes for names, side marks or a hint.
Look for the math

The old page still shows the Java applet. It says that when two equilateral triangles are drawn on the diagonals AC and DB of a shape with AD = BC, their tips P and R coincide, and that this point lies on the bisector of the angle at S. Drag the handles and watch the blue line: on the starting arc the two tips stay stuck together.

A shape made from one circle

A, B and S sit on one circle. C is placed on the line from B towards S and D on the line from A towards S, both the same distance from B and A, so AD = BC. This is what the page calls an antiequilic quadrilateral. The page's opening line calls AD and BC "equal opposite diagonals inclined at 120°"; in the quadrilateral ABCD they are opposite sides, and the 120° is the inscribed angle ASB at the point where those sides meet. The drawn diagonals AC and DB are not equal and are not 120° apart in general; the logic test measures them over thousands of positions rather than repeating that wording.

Why the two tips meet

On the starting arc, ASB = 120°, so a turn of 60° carries the direction of SA exactly halfway to SB. Write S as the origin, let u point to A and v to B with v = rot(-120°)u, and let the equal distance be t. Then A = a·u, B = b·v, C = (b-t)·v and D = (a-t)·u. Turning C about A by +60° and D about B by -60° gives

P = A + rot₆₀(C - A) = (a + b - t)·w
R = B + rot₋₆₀(D - B) = (a + b - t)·w

where w = rot₆₀(u) is the direction of the bisector of angle ASB. The two expressions are the same, so P and R coincide, and the common point is on that bisector. The logic test checks this identity, both equilateral triangles and the equal sides for every dragged position it visits.

The blue line and the hint

The blue segment joins S to T, the point of the circle directly below its centre. Triangle ABT is equilateral, so T is where the two tips meet when C is dragged onto B and D onto A (equal distance t = 0). Tick "Hint" to see the sides AT and BT and their angle marks; the applet draws the same lines. Tick "Side marks" for the matching one-, two- and three-stroke sides of the two triangles.

Where the claim stops

Drag S past A or B onto the other arc. The angle at S becomes 60°, the algebra above no longer applies, and the two tips normally drift apart; the applet itself hides R's name once they are more than ten units apart. The page's claim holds on the arc where the angle is 120°, which is where the applet starts. Our test checks both arcs and reports what actually happens instead of claiming the coincidence is universal.

Try the Hint, then drag S all the way round the circle and watch the status line say when the tips stop meeting.
